newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ready to answer Dole attacks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ready to answer Dole attacks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday said he will use his final debate with Republican Bob Dole to refute personal attacks on him, as aides said Dole may lose votes to third-party rival Ross Perot if he turns mean-spirited.

Dole on Tuesday unleashed his most spirited attack on Clinton of the campaign, saying his opponent has an "integrity gap" and claiming "no administration has been more self-righteous, but few administrations have been more self-serving. No administration has shown more arrogance. But few have displayed more ethical failures."

Asked about the strong attack by Dole, Clinton said: "We'll have time to discuss that in the debate" at 9 p.m. EDT (0100 GMT Thursday) from San Diego -- their final face-to-face exchange before the Nov. 5 election.

The two debates so far -- the first between Clinton and Dole and the second involving Vice President Al Gore and his Republican rival Jack Kemp -- for the most part avoided personal attacks. They also failed to have any significant impact on the lead Clinton has enjoyed for months.
White House Political Director Doug Sosnik insisted that a negative approach by Dole would only cost him votes on Election Day, with Reform Party candidate Perot the beneficiary.

He said that "having Dole pretty much completely abandon even the pretext of a positive message of why you should vote for him" would turn off voters and "the beneficiary of that would probably be Perot."

"I think he'll probably do something that Perot has not been able to do, which is to push his numbers up" in opinion polls, Sosnick said. Perot, whose independent candidacy four years ago generated considerable support, has been unable to create much interest this time around.

Dole's campaign theme on Tuesday was on character issues involving Clinton and his those around him -- challenging the president's assertion upon coming to office that he wanted one of the most ethical administrations in history.

Clinton's ties to Indonesian James Riady have been fiercely attacked by Republicans in recent days, who suspect Riady's influence is behind big contributions to the Democratic Party from individuals with links to an Indonesian financial conglomerate, the Lippo Group.
Clinton on Tuesday deferred to the Federal Election Commission to decide whether the controversial donations should be accepted.

"I believe the political parties should not give back contributions that were legally made and legally received," Clinton said in response to a question about the donations, including $425,000 from a couple who are members of the powerful Riady family, led by Mochtar Riady and his son James.

If the party "made a mistake and took in money that shouldn't have been taken they ought to give that back. There are clear FEC rules on this, there's a law on this. That's what we've got a Federal Election Commission for and we know they're capable of doing the job."
Just how aggressive Dole should be in the final debate -- likely to be watched by some 70 million Americans -- has been a subject of disagreement among his strategists.
In 1976, when Dole was the Republican vice presidential nominee, his confrontational style may have contributed to incumbent President Gerald Ford's defeat at the hands of Democrat Jimmy Carter.
Dole has spent much of the campaign season trying to soften the lingering image of him as a "hatchet man," and at least some of his advisers have argued against his leading the attack on Clinton.
